summary:
We built a crop rotation advisor for farms that no soil survey covers.

Most rotation tools assume a soil map, a local extension service, or a paid
agronomist. Thirteen of the twenty-five datasets listed for this challenge stop
at the United States border. The farmers who most need rotation advice are the
ones with the least data about their own land.

Our tool asks for three things a farmer already knows: where the field is, what
grew there last season, and what matters most right now. From a latitude and a
longitude it pulls ten years of daily NASA POWER climate observations, computes
reference evapotranspiration with the FAO-56 Penman-Monteith method, and scores
all 1,645 possible four-season rotations of eight staple crops on water balance,
heat accumulation, nitrogen balance, pest-cycle break and root-depth alternation.

It then explains each recommendation in plain sentences instead of a score.

We tested it on two Mozambican districts with opposite climates. In Chókwè the
crops need 351 mm more water than the rain delivers each season; in Gurué there
are 1,128 mm to spare. The tool gives opposite answers for the two places, which
is the point.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

The farmer opens a web page, picks one of two locations, says which crop grew

last season, and moves four sliders for what matters most: saving water,

rebuilding soil, breaking pest cycles, opening compacted ground. The tool

returns the five best four-season rotations, ranked, each with a short

explanation of why it ranked where it did and what it costs in return.

HOW IT WORKS

1. CLIMATE. For each coordinate we request ten years of daily NASA POWER data

(2015-2024): temperature at 2 m with daily maximum and minimum, corrected

precipitation, relative humidity, wind speed at 2 m, and downward shortwave

radiation.

2. WATER DEMAND. We compute reference evapotranspiration day by day with the

FAO-56 Penman-Monteith equation, using the elevation returned by the API for

atmospheric pressure. Multiplying ET0 by each crop's coefficient (Kc, FAO-56

Table 12) gives what that specific crop would actually need, rather than a

regional average.

3. SEASONS. We define the growing season as November to April, 181 days,

crossing the New Year. Seasons with fewer than 150 days of valid observations

are discarded. Missing values flagged -999 are excluded, not treated as zero.

4. SCORING. We generate every four-season sequence of eight crops (maize,

sorghum, cowpea, groundnut, soybean, cassava, sweet potato, sesame) and score

each on five measures: water shortfall, growing degree days against each

crop's requirement, nitrogen balance (legumes fix, cereals deplete), pest

cycle break by botanical family, and root depth alternation.

5. NORMALISATION. The five measures live on different natural scales, so we

min-max normalise each one across the entire candidate set before applying

the farmer's weights. Without this step the sliders barely changed the

ranking. This was the single most important correction we made.

6. MONOCULTURE. Sequences that repeat the same crop in consecutive seasons are

removed from the candidate set entirely, not penalised. They are not

rotations, and leaving them in distorted the nitrogen scale.

WHAT MAKES IT DIFFERENT

It needs only a coordinate. No soil survey, no sign-in, no server, no install.

That is a deliberate constraint, not a limitation we settled for: it is what

makes the tool usable in the places where rotation advice is scarcest.

It also explains itself. Every recommendation comes with sentences describing

what distinguishes that option and what it gives up, because a farmer cannot act

on a number between 0 and 1.

HOW WE VALIDATED IT

Before writing the scoring engine we wrote down three predictions: that Chókwè

would show a negative seasonal water balance, that Gurué would show a positive

one, and that drought-tolerant crops would rank highest in Chókwè under a water

priority. All three held against the real data.

We wrote the engine twice, once in Python as a reference and once in JavaScript

for the browser, and verified that both produce byte-identical output across all

1,645 rotations. We tested 360 combinations of the interface controls plus the

all-zero-weights edge case.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

Python 3 with requests for data acquisition and the reference engine.

Vanilla JavaScript (ES modules) for the browser engine. HTML and CSS for the

interface. No frameworks, no build step, no backend. Hosted as a static site on

GitHub Pages so that nothing can fail during judging.

WHAT WE DO NOT CLAIM

NASA POWER resolves to roughly 55 by 60 km, so this is district-level guidance,

not field-level precision, and we say so on the page itself. The Kc values come

from FAO-56 and carry high confidence; the growing degree day requirements and

cycle lengths are indicative; the root-depth and nitrogen values are an ordinal

scale we defined ourselves. All three confidence levels are labelled in the data

file rather than presented as equally solid.

Prices and seed cost are not modelled. For a real farmer a market matters as

much as the soil, and that is the first thing we would add.
